planting.note: Plant tubers after soil has warmed following the last frost, setting them 4-6 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil.

directions: Appleblossom is a collarette-form dahlia whose 4-5 inch blooms open in soft watercolor washes of light yellow fading into pale pink, each petal shaded slightly differently. A single outer row of broad ray florets surrounds a shorter collar of petaloids and a central disc, giving the flower its distinctive layered look. Stake the tall, vigorous stems early, since this is a strong, repeat-blooming cultivar prized by cut-flower growers for its long production season. Deadhead regularly to keep new buds coming through to frost.

common_name: Don Hill Dahlia (Burgundy-and-Red Collarette Dahlia with White-Tipped Collar)

planting.note: Plant tubers after the last frost in full sun and moist, well-drained soil; this tall cultivar benefits from staking at planting time.

directions: Don Hill carries 4-inch collarette blooms with flat, broad burgundy outer florets set off by a shorter inner collar of red petaloids flecked and tipped in white, all surrounding a bright yellow disc. Plants reach a substantial height, so set a stake at planting time and tie stems as they grow to keep the top-heavy flower stems upright. Deadhead spent blooms promptly to encourage continuous flowering from midsummer until frost. This UK-raised cultivar holds the RHS Award of Garden Merit for its reliable garden performance.

common_name: Coseytown Honey Pot Dahlia (Golden Collarette Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers once soil has warmed after the last frost, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Coseytown Honey Pot is a collarette dahlia from American hybridizer LeeAnn Huber's Coseytown breeding line, carrying warm honey-gold blooms with a single outer row of flat ray florets around a shorter inner collar of petaloids. Its open, single-row form makes it a favorite with pollinators as well as cut-flower growers who value the airy, uncrowded look collarettes bring to a bouquet. Deadhead faded flowers regularly to keep the plant blooming from midsummer through the first frost. Lift and store tubers over winter in climates colder than USDA zone 8.

common_name: Hillcrest Cheryl Dahlia (White Orchid-Flowered Star Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers after the last frost in full sun and well-drained soil; stake lightly to support the airy, open growth habit.

directions: Hillcrest Cheryl is an orchid-flowered (star-type) dahlia with a single row of narrow, evenly spaced white ray florets that roll inward along most of their length, giving each bloom a crisp, starburst silhouette around a golden disc. The open, airy flower form and prolific branching habit make it a strong performer in cutting gardens and pollinator borders alike. Deadhead spent flowers regularly to keep fresh buds coming through the season. In zones colder than 8, lift and store the tubers indoors after the first hard frost.

common_name: Sophie Taylor Dahlia (Orange-and-Yellow Orchid-Flowered Star Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers after the last frost in full sun and well-drained soil.

directions: Sophie Taylor is a star-form (orchid-type) dahlia whose single row of narrow, involute petals blends orange and yellow tones into a bright, spiky bloom around a contrasting disc. Its uncluttered, single-layer flower form sets it apart from the dense doubles typical of dinnerplate and decorative dahlias, giving it a lighter, more naturalistic presence in the border. Deadhead regularly to prolong bloom from midsummer to frost, and pinch young growth to encourage bushier branching. Lift tubers for winter storage where ground freezes.

common_name: Destiny's Teacher Dahlia (White Orchid-Flowered Star Dahlia Streaked with Wine-Purple)

planting.note: Plant tubers after the last frost in full sun to light shade and well-drained soil.

directions: Destiny's Teacher is an orchid-flowered star dahlia whose narrow white petals roll into tubes along most of their length and are irregularly streaked and speckled with deep wine-purple, so no two blooms are marked quite alike, opening around a warm gold center. The naturally shorter, bushy habit suits containers and front-of-border plantings as well as cutting beds. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the plant producing new buds from summer into fall, and provide light staking if grown in a windy or exposed site. Pollinators are drawn readily to its open, single-layer flower form.
